tldr: Instead of forcing policies to learn geometry from scratch from images, supplying 3D object poses from off-the-shelf perception and learning only execution allows an ultra-lightweight model of just 30K parameters to adapt from simulation to real robots and unseen robot arms without any additional training.
hero_caption: The same policy running in a simulated environment (left) and on a real robot (right). By mediating through object poses and geometric relationships estimated by vision models instead of generating actions directly from raw pixels, it achieves zero-shot transfer to a real robot and adaptation to unseen robot embodiments.
overview:
In recent robot manipulation, end-to-end learning that maps camera images directly to robot actions—especially large Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models—has become the mainstream. However, attempting to learn 3D environmental geometry, spatial relationships between objects, and robot kinematics entirely from raw pixels requires massive amounts of data and compute. It also introduces severe vulnerabilities, often failing when lighting, camera viewpoints, or the robot's visual appearance change even slightly.

The authors pose a fundamental question: in an era where accurate object pose estimators and robot kinematic models already exist, do we really need policies to learn geometric structure in the first place? Their proposed method, the Screw Attention Policy, cleanly decouples visual perception from action execution. Geometric structure—such as 3D object poses and robot joint information—is explicitly supplied by existing perception tools, leaving the policy model to focus solely on 'action execution' grounded in these geometric relationships. By adopting an end-effector-centric screw representation (a 6D vector unifying translation and rotation) and an attention mechanism invariant to coordinate transformations, the model keeps its learned parameter count down to a mere 30K (30,000).

On the LIBERO benchmark, trained purely on single-arm simulation data, this approach achieved a 96% success rate, matching the performance of massive VLA models. Furthermore, it achieved high success rates under layout variations, across five unseen robot arms, and directly on a real Franka Panda robot—all zero-shot, without any adaptation or fine-tuning. These results suggest that much of what large models were learning at scale was actually geometric structure that could simply be supplied, challenging the prevailing paradigm of robot learning.
contributions: Proposed the ultra-lightweight Screw Attention Policy with only 30K parameters, which explicitly receives 3D object poses and joint screw axes from perception and learns execution alone.
Trained on just 2,000 demonstrations from a single arm in simulation, achieving a 96.0% success rate on LIBERO and 85.8% on LIBERO-Plus under layout variations.

Demonstrated zero-shot transfer across five unseen robot arms without additional training or adaptation, achieving an 80.2% success rate that substantially outperforms prior methods (which peaked at 33.0%).
Deployed the simulation-trained policy directly onto a real Franka Panda robot, achieving 21 successes out of 24 trials (87.5%) across randomized object layouts.

sections.heading: Why force policies to learn geometry?
sections.summary: Conventional end-to-end learning from images wastes model capacity on inferring geometry and kinematics, making it fragile to visual and embodiment shifts. This paper proposes a new paradigm: explicitly supply the policy with geometry from modern perception and robot models, and learn only action execution.
sections.details:
Imitation-learning-based robot manipulation has advanced significantly through the scaling paradigm of expanding dataset and model sizes. However, this has come with enormous data collection costs, heavy computation, and tedious fine-tuning on real hardware. The root cause lies in taking camera images directly as input. Learning end-to-end from pixels means the model must deduce not just task-specific behaviors, but also 3D scene geometry, relative object poses, robot kinematics, and contact mechanics all from raw pixels.

The resulting policies are fragile to changes in the environment or the robot's embodiment. Slight alterations in viewpoint, lighting, background, or the robot's visual appearance often cause performance to plunge. To bridge this 'sim-to-real gap' and achieve 'cross-embodiment' transfer, prior work has relied on collecting diverse multi-robot data or extensive domain randomization. While recent VLAs incorporate 3D foundation models, the core issue remains: policies still dedicate substantial capacity to learning geometric structure.

The authors ask a simple question: if geometric structure is already obtainable, why force the policy to learn it? Modern computer vision can estimate 6D object poses, and robot kinematic models are known. By providing these explicitly as inputs, the policy can ignore textures and camera viewpoints and focus strictly on the geometric relationships defining the task. The Screw Attention Policy achieves this through an end-effector-centric screw representation.

sections.heading: End-effector-centric screws and geometry-aware attention
sections.summary: Object poses and end-effector motions are represented as screws unifying translation and rotation, paired with an attention mechanism that preserves geometric meaning across coordinate frames. The architecture decouples perception/language-based geometric parsing from a 30K-parameter control policy.
sections.details:
### II-A Foundations of Screw Attention
Consider a robot grasping a bowl. To decide the next move, what matters is the relative spatial relationship: the distance, orientation, and pose of the bowl relative to the end-effector. If the entire scene shifts but this relative relationship remains unchanged, the required action is identical. The natural mathematical language for rigid-body spatial relations is the 'screw.' A screw is a 6D vector combining 3D rotational and translational components. Relative object displacements, joint rotation axes, and end-effector velocities (twists) can all be described using the same screw representation.

Between different rigid bodies $i$ and $j$, screws transform across frames via spatial transforms based on relative poses $T_{ij} = (\mathbf{R}, \mathbf{p})$. In Screw Attention, each object serves as a transformer token. When computing attention weights between tokens, the model incorporates not only scalar features but also inner products between screws—specifically geometric invariants known as the Killing and Klein forms. Crucially, learned parameters are never directly applied to the six spatial components of the screws. This guarantees equivariance, meaning the output remains consistent regardless of the chosen reference frame.

### II-B Overall System Architecture
The system operates in two main stages. The front end is a scene parser that combines off-the-shelf perception models (such as CNOS and FoundationPose) with a Large Language Model (LLM). It estimates 6D poses and bounding boxes of objects from camera images and decomposes language instructions into sub-steps (target object, destination, etc.). The back end is the Screw Attention Policy, which receives solely this geometric information. Because it never looks directly at raw pixels, it is inherently robust to visual shifts.

### II-C & II-D Token Representations and Action Primitives
Objects and articulated parts (like drawers) are represented as scene tokens, with articulated parts augmented by joint screws representing rotational or prismatic axes. The end-effector token captures displacements from the hand to the target object along with target grasp and release poses. To explicitly capture manipulation structure, the system includes a module predicting seven action primitives (such as reach, grasp, carry, and place), conditioning the policy on the current phase of execution.

### II-E Output and Control
The policy predicts end-effector twists (linear and angular velocities) and gripper commands over a short time horizon in the end-effector frame, using action chunking similar to ACT. These twists are executed via the robot's Operational Space Controller (OSC). Because outputs are twists defined relative to the end-effector, transferring to a different robot requires no retraining of kinematics; it only requires matching the gripper's stroke.

sections.heading: Outperforming giant VLAs with just 30K parameters
sections.summary: Achieving a 96.0% success rate on the LIBERO benchmark, the method showed remarkable zero-shot transfer under layout shifts, across five unseen robot arms, and onto a real Panda robot. Ablations confirm that feeding poses into a standard MLP is insufficient; screw-based geometric structuring is the key to generalization.
sections.details:
### III-A & III-B Benchmark Evaluations (LIBERO & LIBERO-Plus)
Training uses only the 2,000 human demonstrations from LIBERO (50 per task) and completes in about 2 hours on a single L4 GPU. Total learned parameters amount to just ~30K.
Across the four LIBERO suites, the average success rate reached 96.0%, matching or exceeding state-of-the-art VLA models with hundreds of millions to billions of parameters. When using ground-truth poses from the simulator, the rate reached 97.0%, indicating that perception estimation error had minimal impact. Furthermore, under LIBERO-Plus—which introduces severe perturbations to initial layouts and poses—it retained an 85.8% success rate, rivaling top VLAs despite having a model five orders of magnitude smaller.

### III-C Zero-Shot Transfer to Unseen Arms (LIBERO-Cross10)
The policy trained purely on a single simulated arm (Franka) was deployed directly across five entirely different robot arms. While baseline world-model and cross-embodiment approaches achieved an average success rate of at most 33.0%, this approach attained 80.2% (ranging from 71.0% to 87.0% across the individual arms). This stems directly from reasoning in end-effector-centric geometric coordinates rather than joint angles.

### III-D The Value of Geometric Representation: Why MLPs Fall Short
To address whether the strength comes merely from having object poses as inputs, the authors conducted ablation experiments. Comparing against a 1M-parameter MLP and an equivalent standard transformer given the same poses, all methods scored above ~90% on standard layouts. However, in the LIBERO-PRO suite where object positions are heavily permuted, the baselines plummeted below 30%, whereas this method maintained 74.7%.
Moreover, in an unseen task combining a bowl and a basket ('put bowl in basket')—objects that only appeared separately during training—the baselines failed completely (0%), while this method succeeded 100% of the time. It naturally produced high-clearance trajectory adjustments, recognizing the basket's rim geometry to lift the bowl higher before insertion. The policy also exhibited autonomous recovery: when grasps slipped or objects were dropped, it detected the altered geometric configuration and automatically re-grasped the object in 76% of failure cases without any explicit recovery training.

### III-E Real-Robot Deployment (Franka Panda)
The simulation-trained policy was deployed directly onto a physical Franka Panda without fine-tuning. Inference took just 9 ms on a laptop CPU (well within the 50 ms control cycle). Across 24 trials with randomized object layouts, it succeeded in 21 trials (87.5%). Autonomous retries following missed grasps were also observed on the physical robot.

sections.heading: Supply geometry before scaling up
sections.summary: Supplying geometric structure explicitly and learning only execution enables an ultra-compact 30K-parameter model to achieve outstanding generalization and zero-shot transfer. This finding highlights what manipulation policies actually learn when scaled up.
sections.details:
This work introduces the Screw Attention Policy, decoupling perception from control to learn execution directly from object poses and relative transforms. With just 30K parameters—tiny by modern deep learning standards—it achieves high success on LIBERO, robustness to layout shifts, zero-shot transfer to unseen robot embodiments, and direct deployment to a physical robot.

The message is clear: many capabilities assumed to require massive data and scale emerge naturally when the right geometric representations are supplied from the outset. Rather than forcing policies to re-learn world geometry from pixel inputs, extracting geometry via modern vision tools and letting the policy focus strictly on geometrically grounded execution provides a powerful blueprint for reducing data and compute requirements in robot foundation models.

takeaways: End-to-end learning directly from images consumes most of its model capacity mastering geometry, leaving policies fragile to environmental shifts.

Explicitly supplying geometric data like object poses and joint axes, while learning execution through end-effector screw representations, yields generalization superior to giant VLAs with just 30K parameters.
Defining policies in an embodiment-agnostic, end-effector-relative geometric space enables zero-shot transfer to unseen robot arms and real hardware without fine-tuning.
Geometric attention mechanisms naturally yield emergent behaviors, such as handling unseen object combinations and autonomously recovering from failed grasps.
limitations: Relying on off-the-shelf 6D pose estimators (such as FoundationPose) limits applicability to unknown, unmodeled objects without pre-existing 3D meshes, as well as scenes with extreme occlusions.

Physical robot evaluations remain limited to a single Franka Panda arm across a small set of tasks and 24 trials; evaluations on tasks with complex contact dynamics and diverse hardware setups are left for future work.
Because the framework abstracts scenes into rigid object poses, directly applying it to deformable objects such as cloth or ropes remains non-trivial.
